happened: Congress has not removed maximum employment from the Federal Reserve's goals. On September 16, 2025, House Financial Services Chairman French Hill introduced the Price Stability Act (H.R. 5396), which would do this. It was referred to committee.
closeness: A bill matching the recommendation was introduced, but no committee or floor vote was found, so the dual mandate still stands.
uncertain: Whether the bill had a markup in 2026; one report says it was revived in May 2026, but no vote was found. Newest source: May 2026.

happened: No limit on the Fed's role as emergency lender was found. Instead, Fed officials in 2026 described work to modernize the discount window and make it easier to use. In May 2026 Senators Warner and Kennedy introduced a bill requiring large banks to test-borrow from it.
closeness: The action ran opposite to the recommendation: officials and some lawmakers moved to make emergency lending more ready and less stigmatized, not more limited.
uncertain: Two searches found no 2025-2026 bill or rule to limit the Fed's emergency lending, and no such law is in the project's copy of 2025-2026 laws. Final rules on discount window changes and a reported plan to let banks count discount window access toward liquidity rules were not confirmed. Newest source: September 2026.

happened: The Fed kept shrinking its holdings through 2025, from a peak near $9 trillion in 2022 to about $6.5 trillion. It ended this in late 2025 and began buying about $40 billion of Treasury bills a month to keep bank reserves ample. Holdings were back to about $6.75 trillion by August 2026. New Chair Kevin Warsh favors a smaller balance sheet, but no new reduction plan was found.

key_dates.event: Fed balance sheet peaks near $9 trillion.
Shrinking ends; Fed starts reserve management purchases.

closeness: Some shrinking happened, but it began before 2025 and has stopped. Holdings remain more than seven times pre-2008 levels, and Congress did not limit asset purchases.
uncertain: The FOMC's latest balance sheet decisions (September-October 2026) were not found. Sources are analyst notes, not Fed statements. Newest source: August 2026.

happened: No rule or law limits future Fed purchases to Treasury debt. In practice, all new Fed buying since December 2025 has been Treasury bills: "reserve management purchases" that began at about $40 billion a month and slowed in 2026, plus reinvesting mortgage-bond paydowns into Treasury bills. The Fed has not bought corporate or municipal debt since its 2020 emergency programs ended.

happened: The Fed has not been barred from buying mortgage-backed securities. It has kept letting them run off as they are paid down, and since December 1, 2025 it puts those paydowns into Treasury bills instead of new mortgage bonds. Its holdings fell to about $1.93 trillion by August 2026. It has not sold them.

uncertain: The August 2026 holdings figure comes from a research note. Newest source is August 2026.

happened: The Fed still pays interest on bank reserves; it set the rate at 3.65% in December 2025. An August 2026 analysis says it relies heavily on that rate to steer short-term interest rates. Bills to end the payments were introduced in 2025 (S. 2499 and H.R. 4789 by Sens. Scott and Cruz and Rep. Davidson, S. 2113 by Sen. Paul, and H.R. 146) but none has passed.
closeness: No change yet. Bills in the same direction are pending in committee, and the new Fed chair has voiced related views, but the system has not been changed.
uncertain: No floor vote on the bills was found, and no ending of the payments appears in the 119th Congress laws through October 2026. Newest source is August 2026.

happened: The Federal Reserve has not been abolished. In March 2025 Sen. Mike Lee and Rep. Thomas Massie introduced the Federal Reserve Board Abolition Act (S. 869 and H.R. 1846). No committee or floor action was found.
closeness: A bill in this direction exists, but nothing moved. The chapter itself called this option politically difficult.
uncertain: Bill trackers and searches in October 2026 show H.R. 1846 referred to the House Financial Services Committee and S. 869 to the Senate Banking Committee, with no markup or vote. Newest source: March 2025 (bill text and sponsor release).

happened: No move to back the dollar with gold was found. Earlier gold-standard bills (2022 and 2023) stayed in committee.
uncertain: Two searches found no 2025-2026 gold-standard bill; the last one found was the 2023 Gold Standard Restoration Act (H.R. 2435), which stayed in committee. A 2025 Senate bill (S. 3218) deals with audits of gold reserves, not a gold standard.

happened: In August 2025 the Fed revised its policy framework. Chair Jerome Powell said on August 22, 2025 that the Fed dropped flexible average inflation targeting and its "makeup" strategy and returned to flexible inflation targeting. It kept its 2 percent inflation goal.

key_dates.event: Powell announces revised framework ending average inflation targeting

closeness: The Fed ended flexible average inflation targeting, as the chapter wanted. It did this on its own; elected officials did not require a target range or a planned growth path.
uncertain: Whether Congress considered a bill requiring an inflation target range was not checked.

happened: In November 2025 the Fed, the OCC and the FDIC rescinded their joint climate risk management principles for large banks. In February 2026 the Fed proposed a rule to remove reputation risk from bank supervision and bar using supervision to push banks toward or away from customers for political reasons.

uncertain: Whether the February 2026 proposal has been finalized was not confirmed.

happened: On January 23, 2025, Executive Order 14178 barred federal agencies from creating or promoting a central bank digital currency. In June 2026 Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which bars the Federal Reserve from issuing one through December 31, 2030. It became law on July 11, 2026 without the President's signature.

closeness: Direct match. The law's ban is time-limited (through 2030) rather than permanent.
